prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which established the basis for incretin-based therapies of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: Nothing in the first round weakened the scientific case, and the exchange showed that the disagreement is narrower than it looked. The chain from proglucagon processing and the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide, through glucose-dependent insulin secretion and the effects on appetite and gastric emptying, to drugs with benefit confirmed in large independent outcome trials, is complete, replicated and mature. I keep my preferred configuration: a single part on B028 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The citation rewards what the hormone is, how it acts and in what form it is active, which are the discoveries that defined what any drug had to imitate. That is the discovery the prize tradition is meant to honour. The citation also states the therapeutic consequence, so the physiological prize is not read as indifferent to the medicine. I changed one thing from round 1: I now treat Knudsen as a fully legitimate alternative third name, not only as a fallback, if a majority concludes that the prize should name the step from native peptide to durable drug.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and I cannot remove it with the supplied text. Habener's group contributed to proglucagon and GLP-1 biology and is outside the credited names, so any trio can be called incomplete, and Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is described as contested. Leaving out Knudsen means the prize can be read as passing over the work that made a once-weekly medicine possible, and a prize on a drug class with a very large commercial footprint can be misread as rewarding commercial success. Long-term safety and the durability of weight loss after discontinuation are still being defined, though I do not regard either as a reason to wait.

responses.point: Linnarsson argues that converting native GLP-1 into a once-weekly agent needed new insight (albumin binding, DPP-4 resistance), was not routine engineering, and should be inside the citation, so he names Knudsen as third.
responses.response: This is the best argument for Knudsen, and it moved me. I accept that protraction by acylation and albumin binding was real invention and not routine development, and I withdraw any suggestion that the drug step is merely an implementation of settled biology. I still do not think it outranks identification of the active peptide in a three-name prize, because the pharmacological problem only became well posed once the active form and its glucose-dependent action were known. If you accept that the citation names the therapeutic consequence, the real difference between us is one name, and you have said it is not a point of principle for you. I would ask whether you agree that if the committee cannot support Mojsov's priority from the record, Drucker, Holst and Knudsen becomes the right trio and the citation should then say development explicitly.

responses.point: Svenningsson moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and the chair asks whether the citation should reward physiology only or also the development of long-acting therapies, and how to treat Habener's absence.
responses.response: I agree with the move and with the reasoning that the citation should honour discovery of the physiology and the active form. On the chair's question about Habener, I think the committee must not pretend the omission is absent: the citation should be worded around the physiology and the active peptide, which are the specific contributions of the three named, and not around who first processed proglucagon. The three-name limit is a constraint we did not choose and we should say so in the minutes. I do not think his absence makes the trio indefensible, but it does mean we should not call this trio the complete history of the field, and that is a reason to keep the citation specific.

responses.point: Perlmann raises whether a two-part configuration such as GLP-1 plus the unfolded protein response would be preferable, since B020 has the cleaner attribution but the union would exceed the cap with three GLP-1 names.
responses.response: Arithmetically a two-part prize with three GLP-1 names and two UPR names exceeds the cap of three people, and I do not accept cutting GLP-1 to one name to make space, because that would be the most obvious injustice on the list. Drucker, Holst and Mojsov already use the full allowance. I also do not want to shape a second part just to fit the cap. The UPR deserves recognition for its conceptual clarity, with Walter and Mori as a clean pair, but I would prefer to give it a prize of its own in a year when it does not compete for names. I therefore keep B020 as my first alternative and do not propose a two-part prize.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius worries that B028 has unresolved credit disputes while B045 with a cleaner June and Sadelain pairing has fewer such problems, and cites durable remissions as a stronger maturity case than B020 or B014.
responses.response: I take the maturity point seriously and have moved B045 into my alternatives, replacing optogenetics, because durable remissions in refractory B-cell malignancy are hard to dispute. I do not agree that June and Sadelain is as clean as it looks. Eshhar originated the chimeric receptor and is not credited, and Rosenberg's work is a separate lineage that the credited trio blends together, so we would again be choosing names before agreeing on the achievement. B028 has a contested third seat, but the achievement itself is not in doubt and each of the three named has a documented, distinct contribution. A contested seat inside a well-defined achievement is a smaller problem than an unclear definition of the achievement. I would revisit B045 if the committee were willing to define it around the costimulated chimeric receptor.

responses.point: Sandberg says neither the rule nor precedent excludes an industry-based scientist and that the question is the nature of the contribution, while placing Knudsen first among those he would reconsider.
responses.response: I agree that employment in industry does not disqualify anyone, and that it is the nature of the contribution that matters. That is my own reason for my ordering. Knudsen's contribution was a design solution to a pharmacological problem, whereas Mojsov's, Holst's and Drucker's were findings about what the hormone is and does. Both are real, but a prize that names discovery and states the therapeutic consequence is the better fit. If a majority instead decides that the prize should honour the development, I will accept Knudsen in place of Mojsov and I would not consider that an error.

uncertainties: Whether the supplied record supports Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide well enough to hold the third seat, and how to word the citation so that Habener's contribution is not erased.
Whether a prize anchored in physiology is read as ignoring the protraction work that produced the clinical impact, and whether the citation wording is enough to answer that.
Whether B045 can be defined around the costimulated chimeric receptor lineage, with Eshhar's omission handled, in a later year.
Which alternative should follow GLP-1 if the first trio does not reach four votes, where I currently favour B020 over B045.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal issue applies to any shortlisted ballot. For transparency: I co-authored a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann and a 2019 review with Sten Grillner, and neither is credited on any shortlisted candidate. Optogenetics is topically relevant to motor-circuit neuroscience as a method, which is not a personal or institutional connection to any credited name. I have no documented tie to Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen, Habener, Walter, Mori, June, Sadelain, Rosenberg or Eshhar.
